Metallaphotoredox Synthesis of Axially Chiral Tetrasubstituted
Allenes through Regio- and Enantioselective 1,4-Carbocyanation of
1,3-Enynes

ABSTRACT: Radical 1,4-difunctionalization of 1,3-enynes represents a promising approach for the rapid creation of allenes from
readily available feedstocks. However, the enantioselective synthesis of tetra-substituted chiral allenes from 1,3-enynes via a radical
pathway remains difficult. Herein, we disclose an enantioselective decarboxylative 1,4-carbocyanation of 1,3-enynes through
photoredox and copper dual catalysis, affording a wide array of axially chiral tetra-substituted allenes in a highly chemoselective,
regioselective, and enantioselective manner. This mild and redox-neutral protocol exhibits broad substrate scope and good functional
group tolerance and enables late-stage allenyation of natural and drug-like molecules.
KEYWORDS: asymmetric radical reaction, metallaphotoredox, axial chirality, tetrasubstituted allenes, 1,3-enynes
1. INTRODUCTION
Due to the high reactivity of open-shell intermediates, catalytic
asymmetric photochemical transformations present a significant
synthetic challenge.
1
In recent years, the dual catalysis strategy,
which combines photoredox catalysis with organic catalysis,
2
transition-metal catalysis,
3
or enzyme catalysis,
4
has offered an
efficient solution for constructing chiral molecules. Never-
theless, the synthesis of axially chiral compounds
5
via photo-
induced processes is still in its early stages, with limited examples
reported (Scheme 1a). In their pioneering work, Bach and co-
workers reported a catalytic deracemization of allene lactams
using a chiral bifunctional thioxanthone photosensitizer via a
triplet energy-transfer process.
6
Wu et al. disclosed a photo-
induced asymmetric synthesis of axially chiral styrenes, through
SO
2
insertion and utilizing derived cinchona alkaloids as an
organocatalyst.
7
The Xiao group developed an asymmetric
Minisci reaction for constructing axially chiral heterobiaryls by
combining photoredox and chiral phosphoric acid catalysis.
8
The same group also achieved the formation of various
(hetero)biaryls with axial chirality through the cooperative
photoredox and cobalt catalysis.
9
Subsequently, Li and co-
workers extended the system to the synthesis of axially and
centrally chiral diaryl ethers.
10
Furthermore, the Wang group
developed a photoredox and chromium cooperative catalysis to
prepare trisubstituted chiral α-allenols.
11
Despite these im-
pressive advances, the exploration of novel multiple catalysis
systems for the enantioselective construction of structurally
diverse axial chiral skeletons remains intellectually challenging
and interesting.
Axially chiral allenes are widely present in natural products,
therapeutic agents, and functional materials, and they are also
tremendously useful as intermediates in organic synthesis.
12
Therefore, searching for efficient asymmetric catalytic ap-
proaches to access these molecules has attracted much attention
from synthetic chemists.
13
Given the ready availability of 1,3-
enynes, their asymmetric 1,4-difunctionalization offers a highly
attractive method for the synthesis of chiral allenes.
14

context, most reported methods are focused on the synthesis of
optically enriched di- or trisubstituted allenes,
15
and only a few
examples are applicable to the synthesis of challenging tetra-
substituted chiral allenes via transition-metal catalysis,
16
or
organocatalysis.
17
Recently, 1,4-difunctionalization of 1,3-
enynes via radical pathways emerged as a powerful approach
for the synthesis of tetra-substituted allenes.
18
Nevertheless,
when the enantioselective synthesis is concerned, achieving
good stereochemical control of allenyl radicals is a very
challenging task due to their linear geometry.
19
Very recently,
in their elegant studies of copper-catalyzed asymmetric radical
1,4-difunctionalization of 1,3-enynes, Bao
20
and Liu
21
made use
of radical species that are generated from peroxides and
electron-deficient alkyl halides, respectively. Given the wide-
spread applications of photoredox catalysis in organic synthesis
and the ready availability of various radical precursors, an
enantioselective synthesis of tetra-substituted allenes involving a
photoredox pathway would be highly desirable. It was with this
goal in mind that we initiated this study.
Utilizing dual photoredox and transition-metal catalysis, we
introduced a new approach for site-selective radical difunction-
alization of 1,3-enynes.
22
It is noteworthy that this research area
sees explosive development; numerous strategies relying on the
combination of photo- and electrochemistry with transition-
metal catalysis or organocatalysis have emerged for radical 1,4-
difunctionalization of 1,3-enynes, offering efficient synthesis of
structurally diverse allene products from readily available
feedstock (Scheme 1b).
23−25
However, enantioselective 1,4-
difunctionalization remains a difficult task. Given our con-
tinuous interest in asymmetric photochemical transformations
26
and construction of significant axially chiral scaffolds,
27
we
envisioned that a metallaphotoredox system could be applied to
achieve enantiocontrol over highly reactive allenyl radicals,
leading to the formation of tetra-substituted chiral allenes. The

key in our designed process is the stereoselective trapping of
photoredox-generated allenyl radicals by engaging a suitable
chiral transition-metal complex. Meanwhile, we are mindful of
the inherent difficulty in circumventing the undesired two-
component coupling and 1,2-addition to 1,3-enynes.
28
Herein,
we disclose an enantioselective synthesis of tetra-substituted
allenes via decarboxylative 1,4-carbocyanation of 1,3-enynes
under cooperative photoredox and copper catalysis (Scheme
1c).
2. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
We initiated our investigation by choosing 1,3-enyne 1a as the
model substrate, N-hydroxyphthalimide (NHPI) ester 2a as the
radical precursor, and TMSCN as the nucleophilic reagent, and
the results are summarized in Table 1. A series of commercially
available chiral bisoxazoline (Box) ligands were first examined
(for details, see the Supporting Information), in the presence of
5 mol % Cu(CH
3
CN)
4
PF
6
and 1 mol % fac-Ir(ppy)
3
in DMAc
under irradiation with blue LEDs at 45 °C. Notably, the
common neutral Box ligands that worked well in radical
cyanation
29
led to poor asymmetric induction (L1−L4). In
contrast, the anionic cyanobisoxazoline (CN-Box) ligands (L5−
L8) turned out to be effective. The CN-Box L8 was quickly
established as the best ligand, forming the desired chiral tetra-
substituted allene in 85% yield and good enantiomeric control
(91.5:8.5 er). The subsequent solvent screening was followed,
and DMPU was identified to be the solvent of choice, and the
enantiomeric ratio was improved to 93.5:6.5 (entries 1−4).
Reaction optimization by varying the reaction temperatures was
followed (entries 5−7). Even though the running reaction at 0
°C slightly improved the enantioselectivity, the yield of the
reaction dropped significantly. Other reaction parameter, such
as copper salts, photo photosensitizers, light source, and the
ratios of reactants were all carefully evaluated (for details, see the
Supporting Information). Finally, lowering the photosensitizer
fac-Ir(ppy)
3
loading to 0.15 mol % further enhanced the er ratio
to 96.5:3.5, with virtually maintained high yield (entry 8), which
was attributed to the slow racemization of the allene product
under 1 mol % photosensitizer (for details, see the Supporting
Information). As anticipated, control experiments confirmed
that the CN-Box/Cu
I
catalyst, photosensitizer, and light were all
essential for achieving the desired transformation (entry 10).
After the optimized reaction conditions were established, the
substrate scope with regard to 1,3-enynes was then investigated.
As shown in Table 2, various substituents on the phenyl ring that
was connected with the double bond of enynes were well-
tolerated, forming tetra-substituted allenes in good to excellent
yields with excellent enantiomeric controls (3a−3h). Notably,

1,3-enynes bearing para-, meta- and ortho-methoxy-substituted
phenyls all worked, suggesting that the steric hindrance of the
substituents is inconsequential (3a, 3i, and 3j). 1,3-Enynes with
a di- and trisubstituted aryl moiety also proved to be good
substrates (3k and 3l). Moreover, enynes containing a
heterocycle, e.g., 1,3-benzodioxole, or thiophene, worked
equally well for the reaction, and the desired allenes were
obtained in high yields with good enantiomeric controls (3m
and 3n). When a naphthyl-containing 1,3-enyne was employed,
the enantioselectivity of the reaction dropped significantly (3o).
The alkynyl moieties of 1,3-enynes were next examined. The
methyl and linear alkyl substituents of different lengths, as well as
the cycloalkyl groups, were all well-tolerated (3p−3s). When the
cyclohexyl group was directly attached with the alkynyl moiety,
the desired product was obtained in an acceptable yield and er
value (3t). However, the employment of 1,3-enyne with a
sterically hindered tert-butyl group led to a much reduced
enantiomeric control (3u). Finally, 1,3-enynes with an alkyl
chain decorated with different functional groups, e.g., chlorine,
silyl ether, and esters, were good substrates as well, and the allene
products were obtained in good yields with excellent er values
(3v−3y).
The substrate scope with regard to redox-active alkyl esters
was next examined (Table 3). A broad range of NHPI esters 2
derived from primary, secondary, and tertiary alkyl carboxylic
acids were employed. Primary alkyl groups of different chain

Secondary alkyl carboxylic acid-derived NHPI esters were
also shown to be suitable substrates (4j−4p). Five- and six-
membered cyclic-acid-derived NHPI esters were excellent
substrates, forming enantiomerically enriched allene products
containing cyclohexyl, pyran, and piperidine moieties. In
contrast, the cyclopropyl substrate was less ideal (4k). Lastly,
a number of highly sterically hindered tertiary alkyl NHPI esters
were also investigated, and it is intriguing to notice that the tetra-
substituted allenes bearing very sterically demanding groups
were obtained in high yields and excellent enantioselectivities
(4q−4u). It is noteworthy that difunctionalization protocol of
1,3-enynes reported herein is regiospecific; we did not observe
any 1,2-addition byproducts during the reaction.
Alkyl carboxylic acid structures are widely present in natural
products and drug molecules; thus, late-stage allenylation
reaction was performed, leading to the generation of complex
allene structures (Table 3). Exposure of glycine-derived ester
afforded allene 4v in a good yield. Fatty acids, including lauric
acid and oleic acid, were readily converted to the corresponding
allene products in good yields with excellent enantioselectivity
(4w and 4x). Moreover, alkyl carboxylic acids derived from drug
molecules, such as gemfibrozil (4y), gabapentin (4z), oxaprozin
(4aa), menbutone (4ab), and fenbufen (4ac), could all be
employed in this asymmetric 1,4-carbocynation reaction of 1,3-
enynes. In particular, the functional group tolerance of this
protocol has been fully demonstrated; highly functional drug
molecules, e.g., bezafibrate (4ad), mycophenolic acid (4ae), and
dehydrocholic acid (4af) smoothly formed the allenylation
products.
Synthetic applications of allene products are illustrated
(Scheme 2). A gram-scale synthesis of tetra-substituted allene
3a was performed under the standard reaction conditions.
Under basic conditions, allenyl cyanide 3a was readily
hydrolyzed to allenamide 5 without enantiomeric erosion. The
selective reduction of 3a with diisobutylaluminum hydride
(DIBAL-H) afforded 6 with a 95:5 er, which could be further
transformed to allenyl alcohol 7 and the analogue of insect
pheromone 8 via a Wittig reaction. In addition, the transfer of
axial chirality to central chirality was investigated. Through
copper-mediated cyclizative bromination of 5, highly function-
alization lactam 9 with a quaternary carbon center was obtained
in an enantiomerically enriched form. Treating allenyl alcohol 7
with NBS led to the creation of enantioenriched 2,5-
dihydrofuran 10. When 7 was treated with NIS, sequential
electrophilic iodinating cyclization and oxidation in the air took
place, forming iodinated 2-(5H)-furanone 11. The vinyl
bromide and iodide moieties in the above structures can be
subjected to further cross-coupling reactions, yielding heter-
oatom-containing skeletons with promising biological activ-
ities.
30
A series of control experiments were performed to probe the
reaction mechanism. With the addition of the radical scavenger
TEMPO, the reaction was inhibited. We also detected the
TEMPO adduct 12, indicating the formation of an alkyl radical
species (Figure 1a). Several radical clock studies were carried
out (Figure 1b). The use of NHPI ester 2k with a cyclopropyl
group afforded exclusively ring-opened allene 4e, strongly
suggesting the intermediacy of alkyl radicals. However, when a
1,3-enyne bearing a ring-opening or ring-closing radical probe at
the R
2
position (1s and 1w) was subjected to the standard
reactions, the corresponding allenes 13 and 14 were smoothly
obtained, and the isomerized products 13′ and 14′ were not
observed. These results support that the coupling rate of the
allenyl radical with the copper complex is faster than the rate of
the radical ring-opening and ring-closing reactions. Treatment
of 1,3-enyne 1a and NHPI ester 2a with fac-Ir(ppy)
3
under blue
LEDs afforded Heck-type product 15 in 89% yield, indicating
the existence of the propargyl radical in the reaction. A linear
correlation between the ee values of ligand L8 and the ee values
of product 3a was observed, suggesting that the active catalytic
species is a monomeric copper complex with a single chiral
ligand (Figure 1c). The light on/off experiment showed that the
continuous irradiation was essential for this reaction, and
combined with the quantum yield (φ = 0.23), the radical chain
mechanism could be ruled out (Figure 1d). Furthermore,
fluorescence-quenching experiments were conducted, and it was
found that the excited-state photocatalyst fac-Ir(ppy)
3
was
quenched by NHPI ester 2a, rather than 1,3-enyne 1a and
TMSCN, supporting an oxidative quenching pathway (Figure
1e).

3. CONCLUSIONS
In conclusion, we have developed an enantioselective
decarboxylative 1,4-carbocyanation of 1,3-enynes via photo-
redox and copper cooperative catalysis for the synthesis of axially
chiral tetra-substituted allenes. The reaction is conducted under
mild reaction conditions, without the use of external oxidants,
displaying excellent chemoselectivity, regioselectivity, and
enantioselectivity. The scope of the reaction is broad, applicable

Furthermore, this method is amenable for the late-stage
functionalization of natural products and drug-like molecules.
We anticipate that this metallaphotoredox dual catalysis will
open a new avenue for the asymmetric synthesis of axially chiral
allenes and their applications in organic synthesis and medicinal
chemistry.
4. METHODS
An oven-dried 10 mL sealed tube containing a stirring bar was
charged with 1,3-enyne 1 (0.3 mmol, 1.5 equiv), NHPI esters 2
(0.3 mmol, 1.5 equiv), Cu(CH
3
CN)
4
PF
6
(3.8 mg, 0.01 mmol, 5
mol %), L8 (6.8 mg, 0.014 mmol, 7 mol %), fac-Ir(ppy)
3
(0.2
mg, 0.0003 mmol, 0.15 mol %), and DMPU (2.0 mL, 0.1 M)
under a nitrogen atmosphere, and then TMSCN (0.2 mmol)
was added via a syringe. The resulting mixture was stirred for 12
h under irradiation with blue strip at 45 °C. After completion of
the reaction, the resulting mixture was diluted in EtOAc,
transferred to a 125 mL separatory funnel, washed with brine,
dried over anhydrous MgSO
4
, and concentrated by rotary
evaporation. The residue was purified by column chromatog-
raphy on silica gel or thin-layer chromatography on silica gel
using petroleum ether/ethyl acetate as an eluent to afford the
corresponding allene products.
